events.title: Proposed ruling: escalate (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
The case was filed as a safety dispute and the complaint ("threatened to lock me in when I asked to get out"; "felt unsafe for the whole ride") is on its face a threat and a feeling-unsafe allegation, which is a safety indicator under SAFE-1. The trace marks the SAFE-1 screen as settled (✓) with the only allowed outcome being escalation, so I do not rule on the merits.

Reading the chat: at 21:36 the rider wrote "Please stop the car, I want to get out here." [F3] and the driver replied "Sit down or I lock the doors." [F4]. In context these are a request to exit the moving vehicle and a driver statement about locking the doors rather than stopping — on the face of it an intimidation/detention-type allegation, and at minimum an abuse-of-conduct concern under SAFE-1; the complainant's statement that she felt unsafe for the whole ride reinforces the indicator. The driver's account — that the rider was drunk and tried to open a door on Clemenceau Avenue and he told her to sit down for her own safety and drove on to the destination [F6] — is a competing explanation for the same words, written after the trip and not part of the timestamped chat [F5]. Which account is true is a fault question, and SAFE-3 forbids this court from determining fault or recommending an outcome in a safety case. Because the dispute type is safety and the screen is positive, the ruling is escalate: a human reviewer, not this court, decides.

On whether the record is complete enough to support a non-safety outcome: the trip data are clean — 15.4 km actual against 15.5 km optimal (−0.1 km) [F1] and 20.7 min against 21.8 min estimated [F2] — so no route-deviation refund arises under RD-1 and no amount is quantified from the fare side. The chat record is complete and every message timestamped [F5]. What is not settled by any record is the underlying conduct (whether a door was opened, whether the rider was intoxicated, whether the doors were actually locked, and why the driver did not stop) — but that gap does not change the path here: the safety screen already routes this to a person, so the escalation stands on SAFE-1 and SAFE-3 rather than on the missing-evidence rule.

Safety screen: the chat, the complaint and the driver's statement were read. The screened material contains the driver's "Sit down or I lock the doors." [F4] answering the rider's request to be let out [F3], plus the complaint's allegation of feeling unsafe; this is a safety concern. No accident or injury is recorded and no 995-type event appears [F1, F2]. The safety finding is recorded as suspected because, on the words alone, the meaning of the driver's message is contested between the rider's reading (a threat) and the driver's explanation [F6], and the reviewer must weigh it. No fault or outcome is stated or implied for either party, per SAFE-3.

Amounts: escalation carries no monetary award, so amount is null. No account flag or credit is set: RD-6/NS-2/NS-9 conditions are not met on this record (no upheld deviation, no no-show fee, no repeat no-shows) [F7, F8], and SAFE-3 bars this court from recommending interim measures under SAFE-4. Profiles [F7, F8] were checked only for those threshold conditions and did not decide anything.

claims.assertion: The driver's own words in the in-app chat are a threat to lock the rider in the vehicle: at 21:36 the rider asked "Please stop the car, I want to get out here." and the driver answered "Sit down or I lock the doors."

The rider communicated a wish to leave the ride and felt unsafe for the remainder of the trip, so the case contains a safety indicator (threat / feeling unsafe) and must go to a human reviewer; the AI may not rule on fault or outcome.

The threat is not diminished by the driver's post-trip explanation: his written statement admits he 'did not stop until the destination', i.e. he refused the rider's request in F3 and kept her in the car, and the statement is not part of the timestamped chat record.

This is not a fare or route case: the GPS track shows actual distance 15.4 km against an optimal 15.5 km (-0.1 km, -1%) and duration 20.7 min against 21.8 min, so no route-deviation refund arises and the entire complaint is the safety conduct.

The rider has 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days over a 520-day account, so the complaint is not a repeat-claim pattern; the driver's long record (2100 days, 1204 trips, 0 upheld) is noted but cannot decide a safety allegation.
Pending human review, the safety screen permits interim measures against the accused party, and the file should be escalated with the chat record (2 timestamped messages) attached.

weaknesses: The driver's statement (F6) offers a benign reading of the same words: that F4 was said 'for her own safety' after the rider tried to open the door at the lights on Clemenceau Avenue — the judge may read F4 as a safety instruction rather than a threat, so the SAFE-1 reading rests on the words of F3-F4 alone.

There is no GPS or timeline record of the door incident, no call recording, and no record that the driver actually locked the doors; only the chat and the driver's untimestamped statement exist, so the surrounding conduct is undetermined (TH-4 may be raised).
No injury or accident is recorded and no fare/route irregularity exists (F1, F2), so apart from escalation there is no monetary refund I can quantify from a fare or GPS fact.

claims.assertion: This is a safety-type dispute: the complaint, "The driver threatened to lock me in when I asked to get out. I felt unsafe for the whole ride", alleges a threat and states the rider felt unsafe, so the record must go to a person and SAFE-3 bars this court from ruling on fault or outcome.

The driver is not a stranger risk: 5.8 years on the platform, 4.9 rating, 1204 trips in 90 days, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days (F8), against a rider profile of 4.8 with 0 disputes (F7) — no pattern of misconduct on the driver's side supports any adverse finding on the safety question.

The only contemporaneous driver text is F4 (21:36) answering the rider's F3 (21:36) request to stop; the driver's explanation, that the rider tried to open a door at lights on Clemenceau Avenue and he told her to sit down for her own safety and drove on to the destination (F6), is a safety rationale for not stopping mid-carriageway — it is a claim to be weighed by the human reviewer, not a finding for this court, because there is no call recording and no independent record of the door incident.

The chat record is complete and timestamped — 2 messages, every one timestamped (F5) — so the exchange F3/F4 is the whole in-app conversation and the case file is complete on the messaging point; what remains undecidable (whether the door was opened, whether the rider was intoxicated) is exactly the kind of contested account SAFE-1/SAFE-3 send to human review rather than to a system ruling.

There is no route or fare irregularity to add to the complaint: actual distance 15.4 km vs optimal 15.5 km, i.e. -0.1 km (-1%) (F1), and duration 20.7 min vs estimated 21.8 min (F2), so the trip was driven on the shortest line available and 1.1 min quicker than estimate — the driver gained nothing and the rider was not over-carried.

weaknesses: The driver's own words quoted by the rider — F4: "Sit down or I lock the doors." — read on their face as a threat and are the strongest fact against us; they are a driver message that matches the complaint's wording almost exactly.

F3 shows the rider asked to be let out at 21:36 and the driver did not stop until the destination (F6 admits this), so on the record the rider was kept in a moving car after a clear request to exit — the human reviewer may treat that as detention regardless of the driver's safety rationale.

The door-opening incident the driver relies on exists only in F6, his own post-trip statement, with no call recording and no GPS or video fact corroborating it; under the rule that statements lose to system records, it does not outrank the rider's account.

There is no traffic or fare fact set for this case (both tools returned no facts), so the driver cannot point to an objective reason (congestion, one-way road) why stopping at that point on Clemenceau Avenue was unsafe.
The driver's 4.9 rating and 5.8-year history (F8) cannot decide the safety question, and the rider's clean profile (F7, 0 disputes in 90 days) removes the 'habitual complainer' angle.

points.response: Agreed without reservation: the complaint's words (threat, feeling unsafe) and the driver's F4 text bring this under SAFE-1's mandatory human screen, and under SAFE-3 neither advocate's court may rule on fault — the file goes to a person with the chat attached.

The driver's 5.8-year history, 4.9 rating and 1204 trips with zero disputes cannot answer a one-off safety allegation and does not decide the safety question; the same is true of my client's clean 4.8 profile (F7), so the profiles (F7, F8) are neutral on the threat itself and only bear on credibility for the human reviewer.

The opponent concedes F6 is an uncorroborated post-trip claim with no call recording, and F5 shows the timestamped in-app record contains only the rider's exit request and the driver's "Sit down or I lock the doors." (F3, F4); the safety rationale therefore rests on a statement alone and does not outrank the contemporaneous words.

F5 confirms the chat is complete and timestamped, which strengthens rather than weakens the rider's case: the only in-app exchange is the request to stop and the threat about the doors (F3, F4), with nothing in the record describing a door being opened or a hazard; the contested matters go to the reviewer, not to a system ruling.

We do not contest the driving line: F1 shows 15.4 km actual against 15.5 km optimal and F2 shows 20.7 min against 21.8 min estimated, so no route-deviation refund is sought; the complaint is purely the safety conduct of refusing the exit request (F3, F4, F6).

The words in F4 are quoted verbatim by F3 and are the rider's own contemporaneous quote; I do not dispute the wording, but who said what and what it meant is a finding of fault that this court is forbidden to make — F4 and F6 give two competing accounts of one exchange and SAFE-1/SAFE-3 send exactly that to a person, not to a system ruling.

Conceded: the complaint alleges a threat and that the rider felt unsafe for the whole ride, so a safety indicator is present (F3, F4) and the case goes to a human reviewer under SAFE-1, with SAFE-3 barring this court from ruling on fault or outcome — which is the escalation both sides now ask for.

F6 is the driver's post-trip written statement and not part of the timestamped chat (F5) — I accept that — but the rider's own case turns on those same words in F4, and with no call recording and no record of the door incident the surrounding conduct is undetermined (F5, F6): neither account wins on this record, so the human reviewer takes the file under SAFE-3, not a finding for the rider.

Conceded: with 15.4 km actual against 15.5 km optimal (F1) and 20.7 min against 21.8 min estimated (F2), the trip is inside RD-1 tolerance and no route-deviation refund arises — the only contested matter is the safety allegation.

Agreed that profiles cannot decide a safety case on either side — F8 (2100 days, 1204 trips, 4.9, 0 upheld) shows no pattern of misconduct and F7 (520 days, 0 disputes) shows no repeat-claim pattern, so I withdraw profile as a ground for any finding and ask only that the file be prepared for, and sent to, a human.

I do not contest escalation with the chat record attached (F5: 2 messages, every one timestamped), but SAFE-4 interim suspension is for the human reviewer to decide after reading F4 against F6 and the rider's complaint — SAFE-3 forbids this court from recommending action against either party, and F6 explains F4 as a safety instruction, so no suspension should be presumed from the exchange alone.
